meaning: 'Awakening-being' — one who vows Buddhahood for the sake of all beings

phonemes.desc: Long o like 'bode' — the awakening (bodhi) opening the word, heavy and stressed.
The aspirate dh, a voiced breath — bodhi, 'awakening,' the root of the whole compound.
Dental sattva, 'being, essence' — with the long ā lost even in the standard spelling: it is bodhi-sattva, an 'awakening-being.'

pronunciation.approximation: 'BOH-dhi-sut-tuh' — stress on BOH; the dh is a voiced breath; the final va is a soft 'wuh.'

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: bodhi 'awakening' + sattva 'being, essence' — 'one whose being is awakening' (Monier-Williams); the long ā of sattva is etymological but conventionally unmarked

kin.label: Pāli
kin.form: bodhisatta — the canonically attested form, used of Gotama before his awakening

kin.label: Tibetan
kin.form: byang chub sems dpa' — 'hero of the awakening mind,' the standard translation across the Tibetan canon

pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Bodhisattva' is ASCII-canonical in spelling. The scholarly restoration adds the knowledge the spelling hides — the long ā of sattva and the compound's meaning: not 'enlightenment-being' in the abstract but a being whose essence is a specific, nameable awakening.

domains.title: Bodhisattva
domains.subtitle: The Awakening-Being — the Vow That Refuses the Exit
domains.lead: A bodhisattva is a being who has vowed awakening for the sake of all beings — and who, by that vow, defers the exit: not final nirvāṇa while a single being remains unliberated. The Mahāyāna made the word its founding institution: the bridge from one man's awakening to a vocation open to everyone.

cards.name: The Vow
cards.desc: Praṇidhāna — 'may I not sit on awakening's seat until every being is freed' — the founding act of the bodhisattva career.

cards.name: The Ten Stages
cards.desc: The Daśabhūmikasūtra's bhūmis — from Joyful to Dharma-Cloud — enlightenment surveyed as a climbable landscape.

cards.name: The Perfections
cards.desc: The six pāramitās — giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom — the curriculum every vow must pass through.

cards.name: The Exemplars
cards.desc: Avalokiteśvara hearing the world's cries, Kṣitigarbha vowing the hells be emptied — compassion walking in person.

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Untouched by the mud it grows from — the bodhisattva in the world but not of its stain; also Padmasambhava's birthplace, the word made landscape

symbols.name: The sword of wisdom
symbols.meaning: Mañjuśrī's blade cutting through ignorance — insight wielded not for oneself but to clear the road for others

symbols.name: The water flask and willow
symbols.meaning: Guanyin's healing emblems — the nectar of compassion poured drop by drop onto specific suffering

symbols.name: The moon in water
symbols.meaning: The bodhisattva's presence as reflection — appearing to beings in whatever form frees them, without ever leaving the empty sky

symbols.name: The staff that shakes the six realms
symbols.meaning: Kṣitigarbha's iron khakkhara — its rings wake the dead; his vow keeps him in hell's doorway until it is empty

mythology.lead: The bodhisattva is the Mahāyāna's answer to its own founder's stunning success: if one man woke, the door was never locked. Its mythology runs from the Pāli canon's bodhisatta — Gotama's pre-awakening selves — to cosmic vows that hold the door open for everyone else.

myths.title: An Awakening-Being, Not Yet a Buddha
myths.text: The word is a compound: bodhi, awakening, plus sattva, being — "one whose essence is awakening." In the Pāli canon bodhisatta is a technical term for the Buddha before his awakening: the Nidānakathā and the Mahāpadāna Sutta (DN 14) use it of Gotama's past lives, from the bodhisatta enthroned in Tuṣita down to the last birth at Lumbinī. The Mahāyāna inverted the lens: the bodhisattva is no longer the road one man walked but a vocation open to all — one who deliberately defers final nirvāṇa until the grass of beings is dry, in the Sanskrit formula of the Kāraṇḍavyūha. The compound thus carries an entire schism in six syllables: the earlier tradition's biography against the later tradition's program. An awakening-being is the answer of a religion to its own founder's success: if one man woke, the door was never locked.

myths.title: The Promise That Builds a Bridge
myths.text: Everything begins with a vow. The Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra — the final book of the Avataṃsaka — sends the pilgrim Sudhana through fifty-three teachers and ends inside Maitreya's tower, where past vows stand visible as architecture, each floor a former life; the praṇidhāna, "may I not sit on awakening's seat until every being is freed," is the bodhisattva's founding act. Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra (8th c.) gives the vow its classic liturgy: "For as long as space endures, and for as long as beings remain, may I too abide, to dispel the misery of the world." The jātakas test the vow against the body itself — Prince Śibi giving his eyes to the hawk (Jātaka 499), Vessantara giving away his wife and children (Jātaka 547). The mythic kernel: a promise made not to a god but to the uncountable future — compassion as a contract written across lifetimes, signed before any power existed that could enforce it.

myths.title: From Joyful to Dharma-Cloud
myths.text: The Daśabhūmikasūtra maps the bodhisattva career as ten bhūmis, each a world of its own. Pramuditā, Joyful: the first glimpse, irreversible; Vimalā, Stainless, where the ten courses of action are purified; Prabhākarī, Luminous, where the factors of awakening blaze; Arciṣmatī, Blazing; Sudurjayā, Difficult-to-Conquer; Abhimukhī, Facing — the turn toward suchness; Dūraṅgamā, Gone-Afar; Acalā, Immovable, where nothing mundane can shake the vow; Sādhumatī, Good-Intelligence; and Dharmameghā, Dharma-Cloud, where Buddhas of the ten directions pour consecration from their crowns and the bodhisattva can rain the Dharma like a storm. The scheme seeded every later system — the five Maitreya treatises' summaries, the Tibetan graded paths, the Huayan's own rounds. Its meaning: enlightenment is not a moment but a landscape, surveyed in advance so that travelers can know exactly where they stand.

myths.title: Avalokiteśvara and the Great Vows
myths.text: The bodhisattva ideal walks in person. In the Lotus Sūtra (ch. 25) Avalokiteśvara hears the cries of the world and appears in whatever form frees — to the drowning as a boat, to the burning as rain, "with these many bodies wandering in the samsaric world"; Kṣitigarbha takes the opposite route, his vow driving him down — "not until the hells are empty will I become a Buddha" (Kṣitigarbha Sūtra); Mañjuśrī carries wisdom, Samantabhadra practice, Maitreya the future. Tibetan hagiography pushes the idea to its limit: overwhelmed by the sight of unending suffering, Avalokiteśvara shatters into a thousand pieces, and Amitābha reassembles him with eleven heads and a thousand arms — compassion that had to be rebuilt to keep going. The exemplars make the abstract inspectable: a vow you can picture, walking through fire and down into hell on your behalf.

lore.syncretism: The bodhisattva was Buddhism's great export. In China the male Avalokiteśvara became Guanyin, the most beloved goddess of East Asia — a transformation paralleled in Japan's Kannon and Korea's Gwan-eum, each culture finding in the vow the compassion it needed. Hinduism quietly adopted the figure: the Laṅkāvatāra-era Nārāyaṇa passages echo the Nārāyaṇa of the epics, and bodhisattva-like figures such as Hanumān in later bhakti are hard to imagine without the model. The Jesuits meeting Tibetan Buddhism classified the bodhisattvas as "Buddhist saints"; Romantic scholarship made them "altruistic saints of the East"; modern chaplaincy and engaged Buddhism have made the vow itself — beings are numberless, I vow to free them — a secular covenant recited in zendos, cathedrals, and hospitals. The word outgrew its religion and became a description of a human possibility: awakening on behalf of others.
lore.culturalLegacy: The bodhisattva is the most painted figure in Buddhist art after the Buddha himself — Guanyin's white-robed thousand-armed forms fill the caves of Dunhuang and the museums of the world; Samantabhadra rides his elephant across China's sacred mountains; Jizō's red-bibbed statues line every Japanese roadside, guardian of dead children. The vow's four lines — beings are numberless, I vow to free them; delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them — open every sesshin on earth. In the West the word entered the language through the Beats and the Engaged Buddhism of Thich Nhat Hanh, who translated the vow into antiwar action: the bodhisattva, he wrote, is one who postpones nirvana "to help suffering beings." A term coined to describe one man's past lives now names anyone who refuses to be free alone.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The bodhisattva is the most daring idea in the history of ethics: a moral agent whose deadline is infinity. Ordinary virtue balances cost and reward; the vow sets the reward aside entirely — awakening withheld, deliberately, until the last stranger is free. Logically it is madness; existentially it is the only response to a world of uncountable suffering that does not end in despair or indifference.

And yet the tradition is unsentimental about it. The vow does not float; it climbs — six perfections, ten stages, three incalculable eons. Compassion without method is just grief, the masters said, and method without compassion is just cold. The bodhisattva holds both: the tenderness of Avalokiteśvara and the terrifying patience of Kṣitigarbha, still standing in the doorway of hell, in no hurry to leave. The word asks of everyone who hears it the simplest and hardest question: who are you waiting for?
lore.archaeology: The bodhisattva's archaeology begins where the Buddha's ends. Aniconic reliefs at Bharhut and Sanchi already show the bodhisatta of the jātakas — the Vessantara and Śibi legends carved in the 2nd–1st c. BCE — while the great anthropomorphic bodhisattvas arrive with the Kuṣāṇas: the Maitreya of Gandhāra with his flask, Avalokiteśvara beside Amitābha's triad. The caves of Ajanta (5th–6th c.) give the career its narrative walls — the jātaka cycles painted as the bodhisattva's résumé. Along the Silk Road the type multiplies: the crowned Guanyin of the Tang, the eleven-headed Kannon of Nara's Hōryūji. The figure is, in the end, archaeology of an idea: art keeps finding new bodies for a being who has, by definition, promised not to stop being born.
